title: How the Bible Came to Us
summary: How the books of the Bible were written, recognised, copied, preserved and translated into our languages.
description: Many believers have never asked how the Bible reached them. This course traces the journey: how God's Word was written over many centuries, how the church recognised which books belong in the Bible, how scribes copied them faithfully, and how translators, including the makers of the King James Version, brought them into the languages of the world.
objectives: Explain how the Old and New Testaments were written and gathered
Show how the church recognised the canon of Scripture
Describe how the text was copied and preserved
Trace the history of Bible translation, especially into English and Nigerian languages
outcomes: Describe the Bible's structure: two testaments, sixty-six books
Explain the tests used to recognise the canon
Explain why the Apocrypha is not part of the Protestant Bible
Describe how manuscripts help us know the original text
Outline the story of the English Bible and the King James Version

modules.title: One Book, Many Writers
modules.intro: The Bible is a library of sixty-six books written over about 1,500 years. This week we meet its shape and its writers.

lessons.title: Two testaments, sixty-six books
lessons.body:
The Protestant Bible has 39 books in the Old Testament and 27 in the New. The Old Testament was written mostly in Hebrew, with a few parts in Aramaic. The New Testament was written in Greek, the common language of the Roman world.

About forty writers took part: kings, shepherds, priests, prophets, fishermen, a tax collector and a doctor. They wrote law, history, poetry, prophecy, gospels, letters and apocalyptic visions.

Yet the Bible tells one story: God's plan to redeem a people through Christ. Jesus said the Scriptures "testify of me" (John 5:39).

lessons.title: How the Old Testament was written
lessons.body:
God commanded Moses to write (Exodus 17:14; 34:27). The law was kept beside the ark (Deuteronomy 31:24-26). Later prophets wrote at God's word, and the scrolls were treasured and read publicly (Jeremiah 36:2; Nehemiah 8:1-8).

By the time of Jesus, the Jews recognised a fixed collection, often called "the law, the prophets and the psalms" (Luke 24:44). Jesus and the apostles quoted it as Scripture, never correcting its contents.

This is the same collection Protestants call the Old Testament, arranged differently.

lessons.title: How the New Testament was written
lessons.body:
The New Testament was written within the lifetime of the apostles and their companions, roughly AD 45 to 95. Matthew and John were apostles; Mark worked with Peter; Luke with Paul. Paul wrote letters to churches and individuals.

The apostles knew they wrote with Christ's authority. Paul said his words were "the commandments of the Lord" (1 Corinthians 14:37). Peter placed Paul's letters alongside "the other scriptures" (2 Peter 3:16).

Letters were read in churches and shared between them (Colossians 4:16).

modules.title: The Canon of Scripture
modules.intro: Who decided which books belong in the Bible? This week we learn what the canon is and how it was recognised.

lessons.title: Recognised, not created
lessons.body:
*Canon* means a measuring rod or rule. The canon of Scripture is the list of books that are God's Word.

The church did not *make* books into Scripture. God inspired them; the church *recognised* them, as sheep recognise their shepherd's voice (John 10:27). A book was Scripture the moment God breathed it out.

This matters. Our confidence rests not on a church council's vote but on God, who gave His Word and guided His people to receive it.

lessons.title: Tests the early church used
lessons.body:
In the early centuries, churches asked several questions of a book:

- **Apostolic:** was it written by an apostle or a close companion?
- **Orthodox:** did it agree with the faith already received (Galatians 1:8)?
- **Ancient and universal:** had it been read in the churches from the beginning, widely and not just in one place?
- **Spiritual power:** did it bear the marks of God's voice?

By about AD 367 the bishop Athanasius listed the 27 books of our New Testament, and councils in North Africa (Hippo, 393; Carthage, 397) confirmed the same list.

lessons.title: The Apocrypha
lessons.body:
Roman Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include extra books, such as Tobit, Judith and 1 and 2 Maccabees, called the Apocrypha or Deuterocanonical books.

Protestants, including Baptists and Pentecostal churches such as Deeper Life, do not count them as Scripture, for several reasons: the Jews never included them in their Hebrew Scriptures; Jesus and the apostles never quote them as Scripture; and some teach things contrary to the rest of the Bible, such as prayers for the dead (2 Maccabees 12).

They can be read as history, but not as God's Word. The original 1611 King James Version printed them between the Testaments, clearly separated.

modules.title: Copied and Preserved
modules.intro: We do not have the original papers, but we have thousands of copies. This week we see how the text was preserved.

lessons.title: Careful scribes
lessons.body:
For centuries the Bible was copied by hand. Jewish scribes treated the Hebrew Scriptures with great care, counting letters and lines to catch mistakes. Later scholars called the Masoretes (about AD 500 to 1000) preserved the Hebrew text with vowel marks and notes.

In 1947 the Dead Sea Scrolls were found, including a complete scroll of Isaiah about a thousand years older than the copies known before. It matched the later text remarkably closely, showing how faithfully the Old Testament had been preserved.

God said His word would endure (Isaiah 40:8), and history bears it out.

lessons.title: Thousands of manuscripts
lessons.body:
The New Testament survives in over 5,000 Greek manuscripts, plus thousands of early translations and quotations by early Christian writers. No other ancient book comes close. For most Greek and Latin classics we have only a handful of copies, made centuries later.

With so many copies, scholars can compare them and see where a scribe slipped. Most differences are tiny: spelling, word order, a missing word.

No doctrine of the faith depends on a doubtful reading. Our Bibles faithfully give us what the writers wrote.

lessons.title: Different Greek texts
lessons.body:
Translators work from printed Greek texts based on the manuscripts. The King James Version (1611) used the *Textus Receptus*, based on later Byzantine manuscripts that were the majority in use for centuries. Most modern versions use a text based more on older manuscripts discovered later.

This explains why some verses, such as the ending of Mark (16:9-20) or 1 John 5:7, read differently in some modern Bibles. Christians hold different views on which text is best.

This school uses the KJV for its references. Both families of texts teach the same gospel and the same doctrines.

modules.title: Translated for Every Nation
modules.intro: God wants every people to hear His Word. This week traces Bible translation from Wycliffe to the King James Version and into Nigerian languages.

lessons.title: The English Bible
lessons.body:
In the 1380s John Wycliffe's followers translated the Latin Bible into English by hand. William Tyndale translated the New Testament from Greek and printed it in 1526; he was executed in 1536, praying "Lord, open the King of England's eyes."

Other versions followed: the Coverdale, the Geneva Bible and the Bishops' Bible. In 1604 King James I approved a new translation. About fifty scholars worked for seven years, and the **Authorised (King James) Version** appeared in 1611.

Its language shaped English for centuries, and it is still loved and used across Nigeria today.

lessons.title: Bibles in Nigerian languages
lessons.body:
Missionaries and Nigerian scholars have translated the Bible into many of the nation's languages. Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a freed slave who became the first African Anglican bishop, led early translation work into Yoruba; the complete Yoruba Bible appeared in the 1880s. The Igbo Union Bible followed in 1913, and the Hausa Bible in 1932.

Translation continues today, because "faith cometh by hearing" (Romans 10:17), and people hear best in their heart language.

Revelation pictures worshippers from "every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation" (Revelation 5:9).

lessons.title: Choosing and using a translation
lessons.body:
Translations differ in approach. Some, like the KJV, follow the original words closely (formal equivalence). Others aim to give the sense in natural modern speech (dynamic equivalence). Paraphrases go further and should not be used for careful study.

A good practice is to use a word-for-word translation such as the KJV for study and memory, and to compare other faithful versions when a passage is hard.

Whatever version we use, the goal is the same: to hear God speak and to obey Him (Nehemiah 8:8).

short.model: The canon is the list of books that are God's Word. God decides it by inspiring the books; the church recognised them.

short.q: Why are so many manuscripts helpful?

assignments.title: Answering a sceptic
assignments.prompt: A friend says, "The Bible has been changed so many times that we cannot know what it originally said." Write a respectful, clear answer using what you learned about manuscripts, the canon and translation.

assignments.title: The Bible in my language
assignments.prompt: Find out what you can about the Bible in your own mother tongue: when it was translated and by whom. If no complete Bible exists, explain what is available. Reflect on what it means to hear God's Word in your heart language.
